title: Can household transfers close a recessionary gap?
stem: Answer both parts. Use a labelled economic diagram where appropriate and draw on a real economy you have studied.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how a temporary transfer payment to households can help close a recessionary output gap.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using real-world examples, evaluate the effectiveness of expansionary fiscal policy in raising real output during a recession.

steps.text: A recessionary gap exists when actual real output lies below potential output. A transfer raises recipients’ disposable income. In the national accounts the government is not purchasing output when it sends the transfer.

If households spend some of the transfer on domestically produced goods and services, consumption rises and aggregate demand shifts right. Firms can employ spare labour and capital. Additional incomes may generate further expenditure, while saving, taxes and imports reduce subsequent domestic rounds.

Draw price level vertically and real GDP horizontally. With upward-sloping SRAS, mark the initial equilibrium below potential GDP. Shift AD to the right and mark the higher equilibrium output and price level. Show potential output and the smaller remaining gap. Credit another internally consistent AD/AS model.

steps.text: One defensible judgement is that prompt, targeted fiscal support can protect demand during a recession, but the increase in current output depends on what recipients can buy, how much they spend domestically and whether firms can expand supply.

For example, the US CARES Act in March 2020 authorized first-round payments of up to USD 1,200 for eligible individuals. This raised disposable income directly. A household facing a cash shortage could sustain food purchases, limiting lost sales and jobs. Others could save the transfer or repay debt, weakening the immediate increase in consumption.

The initial US BEA release for April 2020 reported disposable personal income rising 12.9% while personal consumption expenditure fell 13.6% from March. Closures constrained purchases of services. These aggregate changes help explain why more income need not produce an immediate spending rise. They cannot identify how much lower spending would have been without the policy.

Direct public procurement adds to government spending immediately when production occurs, while infrastructure projects may face planning lags. Near capacity, extra demand can raise prices more than output. Where spare capacity and domestic suppliers are available, purchases or well-targeted transfers can produce a larger output response. A supply-constrained recession calls for a different timing or mix.

Use the country, timing and policy mechanism of any accurate real-world example. More than one example is welcome. Weigh speed against the domestic spending response, available capacity and the time horizon. Apply the best-fit band to the whole answer.
